title: The history of the bicycle
text: Today I'm going to talk about the history of the bicycle, which is a good example of how a technology develops through many small improvements rather than one great invention. The first machine that we might call a bicycle appeared in Germany in 1817. It was called the running machine, and it had no pedals at all. The rider sat on a wooden frame and pushed along the ground with their feet. It was popular for a few years, mainly among wealthy young men, but it was banned in several cities because riders kept knocking over people walking on the pavements. The next important step came in the 1860s in France, when pedals were attached directly to the front wheel. These machines were nicknamed boneshakers, because they had iron tyres and the roads were very rough. To go faster, makers then made the front wheel bigger and bigger, which led to the high-wheeler, the famous bicycle with one enormous wheel and one tiny one. The high-wheeler was fast, but it was dangerous. If the front wheel hit a stone, the rider could be thrown over the handlebars. So it was mostly used by athletic young men, and women, who wore long skirts at the time, found it almost impossible to ride. The real breakthrough was the safety bicycle of the 1880s. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that drove the back wheel. Soon afterwards, air-filled rubber tyres made the ride far more comfortable. The effect on society was considerable. For the first time, ordinary working people could travel several miles cheaply, which widened the area in which they could look for work, and even, some historians argue, find a husband or wife. The bicycle also gave women a new kind of independence, and it changed fashion, as women began to wear shorter, looser clothing for cycling.

title: How bees communicate
text: In this lecture I want to look at one of the most remarkable systems of communication in the animal world: the dance of the honeybee. When a worker bee finds a good source of food, she returns to the hive and performs a dance on the surface of the comb. Other bees gather round and follow her movements, and from them they can work out where the food is. There are two main dances. The round dance is used when the food is close to the hive, usually within about fifty metres. The bee simply runs in small circles, first one way and then the other. This tells the other bees that food is nearby, but not in which direction. For food further away, the bee performs the waggle dance. She runs in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and repeats it. The direction of the straight run tells the others the direction of the food, measured as an angle from the position of the sun. And the length of the waggle run tells them the distance: the longer the run, the further away the food. The quality of the food is shown too. If it is particularly rich, the dancer is more energetic and repeats the dance more times, which recruits more followers. This was worked out in the mid-twentieth century by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who won a Nobel Prize for the work. He trained bees to visit dishes of sugar water placed at different distances, and watched the dances that followed. Some researchers were sceptical, suggesting that bees simply followed the smell of the food. It was not until much later, when researchers built a small robot bee that performed the dance, and real bees flew to the place it indicated, that most doubts were removed.

title: Urban heat islands
text: Today's topic is the urban heat island: the fact that cities are often noticeably warmer than the countryside around them. On a calm summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than nearby farmland. There are a number of causes. The first is the materials cities are built from. Concrete, brick and asphalt absorb heat from the sun during the day and release it slowly at night. Dark surfaces, such as roads and roofs, absorb the most. Second, cities have far less vegetation. Plants cool the air through a process in which water evaporates from their leaves, and when trees and grass are replaced by buildings, this cooling is lost. Third, the shape of the city matters. Tall buildings close together create what are called urban canyons, which trap heat and reduce the wind that would otherwise carry it away. And finally, there is waste heat from human activity: from cars, factories and, increasingly, from air conditioning, which cools the inside of buildings by pumping heat outside. The consequences are serious. Hot nights are particularly harmful to health, because the body has no chance to recover, and heatwaves in cities cause many deaths among elderly people. Higher temperatures also increase the demand for electricity, which can lead to power cuts. So what can be done? One approach is cool roofs: painting roofs white or a light colour so that they reflect sunlight. Another is green roofs, where plants are grown on top of buildings. Planting street trees is one of the most effective measures, because trees provide shade as well as cooling the air. Some cities are also replacing car parks with parks, and designing new districts so that the wind can pass through them.

title: The psychology of habits
text: This morning I'm going to talk about habits, and why they are so hard to change. Psychologists define a habit as a behaviour that is triggered automatically by a situation, without conscious decision. Brushing your teeth in the morning is a habit; you don't decide to do it, you just do. Research suggests that a surprisingly large part of our daily behaviour, perhaps as much as forty per cent, is habitual. Habits are usually described as having three parts. First there is the cue, the situation that triggers the behaviour, such as a time of day, a place or a feeling. Then there is the routine, the behaviour itself. And finally there is the reward, the benefit we get, which makes the habit stronger each time. One important finding is that habits are linked very closely to context. This explains why people who move house often find it easier to change their habits: the old cues have disappeared. Researchers studying students who changed university found that their exercise habits changed much more than those of students who stayed. How long does it take to form a new habit? You may have heard that it takes twenty-one days, but that figure has little scientific support. In one well-known study, the average was sixty-six days, but it varied enormously between people and between behaviours. Drinking a glass of water after breakfast became automatic much faster than doing fifty sit-ups. So what does this mean in practice? If you want to build a habit, attach it to an existing cue, keep the behaviour simple at first, and repeat it in the same place. To break a bad habit, the most effective strategy is often to change the environment, so that the cue doesn't appear. Willpower, it turns out, is much less important than we think.

title: Desalination
text: Let's turn now to desalination: removing salt from seawater to make it suitable for drinking and farming. With populations growing and droughts becoming more frequent, more countries are turning to the sea for their water, and there are now thousands of desalination plants around the world, most of them in the Middle East. There are two main methods. The older method is distillation. Seawater is heated until it turns into steam, leaving the salt behind, and the steam is then cooled to produce fresh water. This works well, but heating water requires a great deal of energy, so distillation is mainly used where fuel is cheap. The more common method today is reverse osmosis. Here, seawater is pushed at high pressure through a very fine membrane, which lets water molecules through but blocks the salt. Reverse osmosis uses far less energy than distillation, but the membranes are easily blocked by sand and living organisms, so the water must be carefully filtered first. Desalination has two major drawbacks. The first is cost. Even with reverse osmosis, desalinated water is several times more expensive than water from rivers or underground sources. The second is environmental. For every litre of fresh water produced, roughly one and a half litres of very salty water, called brine, is left over, and this is usually pumped back into the sea. Near the outlet, the brine can harm fish and other marine life, as it sinks to the sea floor. Researchers are working on solutions, such as spreading the brine over a wider area, or extracting useful minerals from it, including lithium, which is used in batteries. Powering plants with solar energy could also reduce their impact on the climate.

title: The origins of paper money
text: In this session we'll look at the origins of paper money. For most of history, money meant coins made of valuable metals such as gold, silver and copper. The problem with coins is that they are heavy. In China, during the Tang dynasty, merchants who travelled long distances began leaving their coins with a trusted dealer and taking a paper receipt instead. These receipts were nicknamed flying money, because they could be carried so easily. By the eleventh century, the government in one province of China had taken over the issuing of these notes, creating what many historians regard as the first true paper money issued by a state. Notes were printed with complicated designs, using several colours, to make them difficult to copy, and forging them was punished severely. However, the system had a weakness. Because paper costs almost nothing to produce, governments were tempted to print more notes whenever they needed money, for example to pay for wars. The result was inflation: as more notes were printed, each one bought less, and people lost trust in them. When the explorer Marco Polo visited China in the thirteenth century, he was astonished that people accepted paper in exchange for goods, and his descriptions were met with disbelief in Europe. Europe was slow to follow. The first banknotes in Europe were issued in Sweden in the seventeenth century, partly because Swedish coins were made of copper and were so large and heavy that they were almost impossible to carry. Even then, for centuries, paper money in most countries could be exchanged for gold at a bank. It is only relatively recently that money has depended entirely on trust in the government that issues it.

title: Sleep and memory
text: Today I'd like to talk about the relationship between sleep and memory, an area where research has advanced rapidly. We used to think of sleep as a time when the brain simply rests. We now know that it is very active, and that one of its jobs is to process the information we took in during the day. Sleep happens in cycles of about ninety minutes, and each cycle contains different stages. In deep sleep, which is more common early in the night, the brain appears to replay recent experiences. Studies in rats have shown that the same patterns of brain activity seen when a rat learns its way round a maze are repeated during deep sleep afterwards. This replay seems to help move memories from short-term storage into long-term storage. Dreaming sleep, which is more common towards the morning, seems to play a different role. It appears to help with creativity, by linking memories in new ways. In one experiment, people who had a period of dreaming sleep were much better at solving a puzzle that required them to spot a hidden rule. The practical implications are clear, especially for students. Staying up all night to study before an exam is likely to be counterproductive, because the material is not properly stored. Even a short nap after learning can improve recall. There is also evidence that what we learn just before sleep is remembered particularly well, so reviewing notes in the evening may be a good strategy. Finally, a word about age. As we get older, we spend less time in deep sleep, and some researchers think this may partly explain why memory tends to decline in later life. Whether improving sleep in older people can slow this decline is now an active area of research.

title: Coral reefs under pressure
text: In this final lecture on marine ecosystems, I want to discuss coral reefs. Reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to around a quarter of all marine species, which is why they are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea. A coral reef is built by tiny animals called polyps, which produce hard skeletons of limestone. Over thousands of years, these skeletons build up into enormous structures. The polyps live in partnership with microscopic algae that live inside their tissue. The algae use sunlight to produce food, which they share with the coral, and they also give coral its bright colours. This partnership is the key to understanding the main threat. When the water becomes too warm, even by just one or two degrees for a few weeks, the coral expels the algae. Without them, the coral turns white, which is known as bleaching, and if the water does not cool down, the coral may starve and die. Mass bleaching events have become much more frequent as ocean temperatures have risen. Reefs face other pressures too. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, it becomes more acidic, which makes it harder for polyps to build their skeletons. Pollution from farms on land carries fertilisers into coastal waters, encouraging the growth of seaweed that competes with coral. And in some places, destructive fishing methods physically break the reef. Scientists are trying several approaches to help reefs survive. Some are breeding corals that can tolerate higher temperatures and transplanting them onto damaged reefs. Marine protected areas, where fishing is restricted, give reefs a better chance to recover. But most researchers agree that, in the long term, reefs can only be saved by reducing the emissions that are warming the oceans.
